Today they practice comparing two homecoming narratives with text evidence, transitions and formal style."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"variation","definition":"a difference from the usual or standard form; in language, wording that is not standard English","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"conventional","definition":"following the accepted rules or usual way of doing something, such as standard English grammar","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"contrast","definition":"to show how two things are different","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"depict","definition":"to show or describe something in a story, picture or other work","tier":"support"},{"word":"rejoice","definition":"to feel and show great happiness","tier":"support"},{"word":"nymph","definition":"in Greek myth, a female nature spirit who lives in a place such as a river, tree or cave","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 370-375"},{"title":"The Odyssey, Book 13 (excerpt)","author":"Homer","pages":"Odysseus recognizes Ithaca"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Spark thinking about what home means and connect it to the heroes' returns students will compare today.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"What Does Home Mean?","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Think about a time you came home after being away. Turn to a partner and describe how you felt and what made that place feel like home."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What makes a place feel like home: the place itself, the people in it, or something else?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think it's the people. When I got back from my grandma's, I was happiest to see my little brother and my mom, not just my room."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Heroes in stories come home too. Today we compare two of them: Percy at the end of Chapter 22 and Odysseus in an ancient Greek poem. You will write about what home means to each."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about three minutes of talk. Take one or two shares and move on; the heavy lifting comes later."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach students to recognize variations from standard English and use strategies to make their expression formal and conventional before they write about the texts.","activities":[{"id":"lab-standard-english","title":"Recognizing Variations from Standard English","minutes":10,"standards":["L.6.1","L.6.1.e"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Writers use different language in different settings. Texting a friend, we might write 'Percy was like, so done with school.' In an explanatory paragraph, we use formal, standard English. A *variation* is wording that differs from the standard. Our strategies are: spot it, reread aloud, then revise to *conventional* language. Look for slang, a shift in verb tense, a missing apostrophe or a vague word like 'stuff.'"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read each sentence below about Chapter 22. With a partner, find the variation and rewrite the sentence in formal, standard English. Sentence 1: Percy was like totally unsure about going back to camp. Sentence 2: His mom pick the school that is good for him, so Percy decides to stay home. Sentence 3: Percy dont know if home is a place or his mom."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I will model the first one. 'Like totally' is slang. I replace it with a precise word: 'Percy was uncertain about returning to camp.' I reread it aloud and it sounds formal and clear."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What variation did you find in Sentence 2, and how did you fix it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'Pick' doesn't match the tense, because the sentence says 'decides' in the present. I changed it to 'picks' so it says 'His mom picks a school that is good for him, so Percy decides to stay home.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What about Sentence 3?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'Dont' needs an apostrophe and 'Percy' needs 'doesn't.' I wrote, 'Percy doesn't know if home is a place or his mother.'"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Keep the focus on strategies, not on correcting students' home language. Frame formal English as the right choice for this task and audience, not as better than other ways of speaking."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"As you write today, use this check: read your sentence aloud, listen for slang or a tense shift, and revise it to be formal and conventional."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students notice differences between informal and formal English and build sentences that add detail with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: Informal is how we talk with friends. Formal is how we write for school. Ask: Which word sounds informal? What is a more formal word? Frames: The word ___ is informal. A more formal way to say it is ___. Expand a sentence with where, when or why: Percy returns ___ (to his mother's apartment / in the summer / because he misses her).","watchFor":"If students only copy the corrected sentence, then ask them to say why the first version did not fit formal writing. If students add details unrelated to the text, then point back to Chapter 22 and ask where, when or why for Percy. Annotate details about Percy's feelings about home, his mother's choices and the decision about where to spend the year. Then read the Odyssey excerpt and annotate Odysseus's joy, his kissing the ground and his prayer to the nymphs. Record your evidence in a two-column chart labeled Percy and Odysseus, with a row at the bottom for What home means."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details in Chapter 22 show how Percy feels about home and what his mother has done for him?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy feels tied to his mom and wants to be near her, but camp is where he belongs too. His mom makes choices to keep him safe and give him a good life, and he has to decide where to spend the year."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details show how Odysseus feels when he finally recognizes Ithaca?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He is full of joy. He rejoices at being in his own land again, kisses the ground and prays to the nymphs. His actions show how much he has longed for his homeland."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is similar and what is different about how each hero returns home?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both heroes have been through dangerous journeys and both care deeply about home. Add adverbials: Odysseus kisses the ground joyfully, in his homeland, after years away.","watchFor":"If students retell the plot without evidence, then ask: Which words in the text show that? Success: students cite at least one detail per hero and state one similarity or difference."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding details in the Odyssey excerpt","tryThis":"Read the excerpt aloud together, pausing after each action so students can underline joy, kissing the ground and prayer."},{"type":"situation","tryThis":""},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to infer why Odysseus prays to the nymphs and what that shows about his values, citing a detail."}]}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"","keyActivities":[],"vocabularyTaught":[],"standardsCovered":[]}}
